cards.q: You store application data in a JSON file that two processes both read, modify and write back. What goes wrong, and what is the failure called?
cards.a: Both read the same starting content, both write the whole file back, and the second write erases the first one's change entirely. This is a lost update. There is no error and nothing in any log — the change simply is not there.

cards.q: Why doesn't a lock file solve concurrent access to a data file?
cards.a: It mostly works until the process holding the lock is killed or crashes. The lock file stays on disk forever with no owner, and the application is dead until a human deletes it. There is no mechanism to release a lock when its holder dies.

cards.q: You write a file and your program returns successfully. Is the data on disk?
cards.a: No. The operating system accepts the bytes into memory and writes them to physical storage whenever it chooses, possibly seconds later. A power loss in that window can leave a file that is half old content and half new, or the right length but full of zeroes.

cards.q: Why does searching a large data file become impossible rather than just slow?
cards.a: Answering any question means reading and checking every record, because nothing in the file knows where anything is. At ten million records you cannot hold it in memory and every query touches everything, so response time grows linearly with data forever.

cards.q: What does it mean that a plain file enforces no structure?
cards.a: Nothing prevents one record having "age": 30, the next "age": "thirty", and a third having no age at all. Every invariant must be re-enforced by every piece of code that ever writes — including one-off scripts and manual edits.

cards.q: Why is "move money from account A to account B" unsafe with files?
cards.a: It is two separate writes. If the process dies between them the money has left A and never arrived at B. A filesystem has no concept of "these two changes happen together or neither happens."

cards.q: Name the five categories of failure that a database management system exists to solve.
cards.a: Concurrency (lost updates), crash safety (partial writes), search (finding data without reading everything), structure and truth (enforced invariants), and partial failure (grouping changes atomically).

cards.q: Why is "it worked fine as a JSON file for months" not evidence that files are adequate?
cards.a: Every one of the five failure modes is load- and size-dependent. Lost updates require concurrent writes, crash corruption requires an ill-timed crash, and scan cost requires volume. The failures are rare-then-constant, not gradual.

cards.q: What is the single structural idea that makes all five problems solvable?
cards.a: Stop letting application code touch storage. One long-running program owns the bytes, and everybody else asks it. That gives you one place where locking, crash recovery, and rule enforcement can live.

cards.q: Why does a soft "we validate in the application" approach fail to guarantee data quality?
cards.a: There is always more than one writer — a second service, a background job, a migration script, a human in a shell. Any rule that lives only in one client is a hope, not a guarantee.

cards.q: What is the difference between data being consistent and data being correct here?
cards.a: Consistency is about invariants the system enforces at every moment. Correctness is about the values being right. A database can only guarantee the first, and that turns out to be enough to eliminate most classes of the second.

cards.q: Why do these problems matter more for a web server than for a script you run once a day?
cards.a: A web server handles many requests concurrently by design, so "two processes modify the same record at the same time" is the normal case rather than a rare race.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Where did Postgres come from, and what does the name mean?
cards.a: It began at Berkeley in 1986 under Michael Stonebraker as the successor to a database called Ingres — post-Ingres, POSTGRES. It originally used a query language called QUEL; SQL was added in 1994 producing Postgres95, renamed PostgreSQL in 1996 and handed to a volunteer community.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Who owns Postgres?
cards.a: Nobody. It is developed by a global volunteer community under a permissive licence, with no controlling company. This is a real differentiator against MySQL (Oracle) and is why there is no "enterprise edition" gate.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the current major version, and how often do releases happen?
cards.a: Postgres 18, released September 2025. The project ships roughly one major version per year, each September, with five years of support.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the default Postgres port and what does the number mean?
cards.a: 5432. It is simply the port the project registered as its default; nothing about the digits is derived from anything meaningful.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the frontend/backend protocol?
cards.a: The documented binary wire format clients use to talk to the server over TCP. You almost never implement it — a driver like pg, postgres.js or psycopg speaks it for you.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is psql?
cards.a: The official command-line client. Connect with psql "postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db".

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Give the four psql meta-commands you use constantly.
cards.a: \dt lists tables, \d tablename describes one, \l lists databases, \q quits. Also \dx for extensions and \di for indexes.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: In Postgres, what is a "cluster"? Why is the word misleading?
cards.a: A cluster is one server process managing one data directory containing multiple databases — it has nothing to do with multiple machines. The distributed sense of the word does not apply.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the data directory?
cards.a: The single directory on disk holding everything the server owns — data files, WAL, configuration — typically something like /var/lib/postgresql/18/main. Often referred to as PGDATA.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Can one connection query two different databases in the same cluster?
cards.a: No. A connection is bound to exactly one database and cannot see another's tables. Cross-database queries require a second connection or an extension such as postgres_fdw or dblink.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is a schema in Postgres, and what is public?
cards.a: A schema is a namespace inside a database that groups tables and other objects. Every database has a default schema called public, which is why most people never think about schemas until they need multi-tenancy or want to isolate extension objects.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is search_path?
cards.a: The ordered list of schemas Postgres searches when you name an object without qualifying it. Defaults to "$user", public. Setting it is how you make a query written against unqualified names resolve to a specific tenant's schema.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is a table, formally?
cards.a: A fixed set of named, typed columns and an unordered bag of rows.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Why is "unordered" important in the definition of a table?
cards.a: Because a query without ORDER BY may return rows in any order at all, and that order can change tomorrow for the same data if the server picks a different plan. Relying on incidental ordering is a bug that appears only in production.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the relational model and who proposed it?
cards.a: Edgar Codd at IBM, 1970. Data is stored as plain values in named columns rather than as pointers between records, so new questions can be asked later without restructuring the data.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: Why does storing values rather than pointers matter practically?
cards.a: Because relationships are expressed by matching values at query time, you can join any two tables on any compatible columns, including combinations nobody anticipated when the schema was written.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the difference between a database, a schema, and a table?
cards.a: Cluster contains databases; a database contains schemas; a schema contains tables. Connections attach to a database; names resolve within schemas.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is a role in Postgres?
cards.a: The unified concept covering both users and groups. CREATE ROLE with LOGIN makes what you would call a user. Permissions are granted to roles, and roles can be members of other roles.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is pg_hba.conf?
cards.a: The host-based authentication file. It decides, per connection type, database, user and source address, which authentication method applies — scram-sha-256, md5, trust, peer. A connection refused before any password check is usually this file.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What does GRANT operate on?
cards.a: Privileges on objects — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on tables, USAGE on schemas and sequences, CONNECT on databases — granted to roles. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES makes grants apply to objects created later.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is the system catalog?
cards.a: The set of tables where Postgres stores its own metadata — pg_class (tables and indexes), pg_attribute (columns), pg_index, pg_stat_activity and so on. They are queryable with ordinary SQL, which is why monitoring Postgres needs no special tooling.

cards.t: Node 1 · A server that owns the data
cards.q: What is information_schema and how does it differ from pg_catalog?
cards.a: information_schema is the SQL-standard, portable view of metadata; pg_catalog is Postgres's own, which is more complete and more accurate about Postgres-specific features. Use the latter when you need the truth.

cards.q: What is the right mental model of a database schema?
cards.a: Not a bucket you put things in, but a set of enforced invariants — statements guaranteed true of the data at every moment, regardless of which client wrote it. If a rule lives in the database it is true; if it lives only in application code it is a hope.

cards.q: How strict is Postgres about types compared to MySQL or MongoDB?
cards.a: Very. Inserting a string into an integer column is an error, not a silent coercion to zero. There is no equivalent of MySQL's historical non-strict mode truncating or defaulting bad values.

cards.q: text or varchar(n) — which is faster?
cards.a: Neither. They are the same underlying type; varchar(n) just adds a length check. Choose a limit only when it is a genuine business rule, otherwise use text.

cards.q: What is char(n) and why avoid it?
cards.a: A blank-padded fixed-length type. It pads values with spaces to length n, which surprises comparisons and wastes space. There is essentially no reason to use it.

cards.q: Why must money never be stored in float8?
cards.a: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums drift by fractions of a cent and comparisons fail. Use numeric, which is exact decimal arithmetic, at some cost in speed.

cards.q: When is float8 the right choice?
cards.a: For measurements and scientific quantities where approximation is inherent and arithmetic speed matters — sensor readings, coordinates, scores — never for anything that must total exactly.

cards.q: timestamp versus timestamptz — what is the actual difference?
cards.a: timestamptz converts input to UTC on the way in and renders it in the session's timezone on the way out. It does not store a timezone. Plain timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no idea what part of the world it refers to.

cards.q: Which timestamp type should you default to and why?
cards.a: timestamptz, always, for any point in time. Plain timestamp loses the information needed to compare two events from different places, and produces bugs when clocks shift.

cards.q: When is plain timestamp actually correct?
cards.a: When the value genuinely is a local wall-clock time with no instant attached — "the shop opens at 09:00 wherever it is" or a date-and-time a user typed that must be shown back unchanged.

cards.q: Why prefer bigint over integer for surrogate keys?
cards.a: A 32-bit integer runs out at about 2.1 billion. Migrating a live primary key from integer to bigint rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock, which is a painful outage you can avoid for free at design time.

cards.q: Name the five constraint types that matter.
cards.a: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, and FOREIGN KEY.

cards.q: What is a CHECK constraint?
cards.a: An arbitrary boolean expression evaluated per row on insert and update — CHECK (price > 0), CHECK (status IN ('draft','sent')). It cannot reference other rows or other tables.

cards.q: What exactly is a primary key?
cards.a: UNIQUE plus NOT NULL, plus the declaration that this column (or set of columns) is the row's identity. Postgres automatically creates a unique index to enforce it.

cards.q: What does a foreign key guarantee?
cards.a: That every value in the referencing column exists as a key in the referenced table. It makes "an order always belongs to a real customer" a fact enforced by the server rather than something application code hopes for.

cards.q: What are the ON DELETE options for a foreign key and what does each do?
cards.a: RESTRICT/NO ACTION (default) refuses to delete a parent with children; CASCADE deletes the children too; SET NULL orphans them; SET DEFAULT points them at the column default.

cards.q: Why is ON DELETE CASCADE something to use deliberately rather than by default?
cards.a: Because a single DELETE can silently remove an unbounded amount of data across many tables, and it can be extremely slow if the child tables lack an index on the referencing column.

cards.q: What is a composite primary key and when is it appropriate?
cards.a: A primary key spanning more than one column. It is natural for join tables ((post_id, tag_id)) and for partitioned tables where the partition key must be part of any unique constraint.

cards.q: What is the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key?
cards.a: A natural key is meaningful data used as identity (an email, an ISBN); a surrogate key is a meaningless generated value (an identity integer or a UUID). Surrogates are preferred because natural keys change and correcting them cascades everywhere.

cards.q: What does NULL mean?
cards.a: Unknown. Not zero, not empty string, not false. Everything strange about NULL follows from that.

cards.q: Why is WHERE col = NULL always wrong?
cards.a: Because "unknown equals unknown" evaluates to unknown, not true, so no rows are returned. You must write IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

cards.q: What is three-valued logic?
cards.a: SQL predicates evaluate to true, false, or unknown. Only rows where the WHERE clause is true are returned, so unknown behaves like false for filtering but not for negation — NOT unknown is still unknown.

cards.q: Why does WHERE status != 'archived' silently drop rows?
cards.a: Rows where status is NULL evaluate the comparison to unknown and are excluded. You need WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'archived' or WHERE status != 'archived' OR status IS NULL.

cards.q: How do aggregates treat NULLs?
cards.a: They skip them. AVG(score) over ten rows with four NULLs averages six values, not ten. COUNT(col) counts non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows.

cards.q: Can a UNIQUE column contain more than one NULL?
cards.a: Yes, by default — two unknowns are not known to be equal. Postgres 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT if you want at most one NULL.

cards.q: What is COALESCE?
cards.a: A function returning its first non-null argument — COALESCE(nickname, name, 'anonymous'). The standard way to supply a fallback for a possibly-null value.

cards.q: What is the difference between SERIAL and GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY?
cards.a: SERIAL is not a type; it is a macro that creates an integer column, a sequence, and a default. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (Postgres 10+) is standard SQL, has cleaner ownership and permissions, and is the modern choice.

cards.q: Why do identity columns produce gaps in the numbers?
cards.a: Sequences are deliberately not transactional — a number handed out to a transaction that rolls back is not returned. Gaps are normal and expected, and are not a sign of lost data.

cards.q: What is a sequence, as an object?
cards.a: A separate database object holding a counter, with functions nextval, currval and setval. Identity and serial columns are just columns whose default calls nextval on one.

cards.q: What does GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY allow that ALWAYS does not?
cards.a: It lets you supply an explicit value on insert, which matters for data loading and migrations. ALWAYS rejects it unless you write OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE.

cards.q: What is a column DEFAULT and what is the most useful one?
cards.a: A value inserted when the statement supplies none. DEFAULT now() on a created_at timestamptz is the one you will write in almost every table.

cards.q: What is the difference between now() and clock_timestamp()?
cards.a: now() returns the start time of the current transaction and is constant within it; clock_timestamp() returns the actual wall clock at the moment of the call and changes within a transaction.

cards.q: What is a domain type?
cards.a: A named type built from an existing one plus constraints — CREATE DOMAIN email AS text CHECK (VALUE ~ '@') — so a rule can be declared once and reused across many columns.

cards.q: If constraints slow down writes, why not enforce everything in the application?
cards.a: Because the cost is small and the guarantee is absolute. Constraint checks are cheap relative to the write itself, and the alternative is trusting every current and future writer, including scripts and manual edits, forever.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does it mean that SQL is declarative?
cards.a: You describe the result you want, not the steps to produce it. The server decides how. Two very different-looking queries can execute identically, and one query can execute in two different ways on different days as the data changes.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What follows practically from SQL being declarative?
cards.a: That "optimising SQL" rarely means rewriting the text. It usually means giving the server better information (statistics), better tools (indexes), or removing something that blocks it from choosing well.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is the logical evaluation order of a SELECT?
cards.a: FROM (and joins), then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. This is not the order you write them in.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: Why can you use a SELECT alias in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?
cards.a: Because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet; ORDER BY is evaluated after, so it does.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
cards.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. HAVING count(*) > 5 is only expressible after grouping.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does an INNER JOIN return?
cards.a: Only rows where the join condition matched on both sides. Unmatched rows from either table are dropped.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
cards.a: Every row from the left table, with the right side's columns filled with NULLs where nothing matched. This is what you want for "all customers and their order count, including customers with none."

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is the classic LEFT JOIN bug?
cards.a: Putting a condition on the right-hand table in WHERE instead of in the ON clause. The NULL-filled rows fail the condition and are discarded, silently turning the left join into an inner join.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a FULL OUTER JOIN?
cards.a: A join keeping unmatched rows from both sides, NULL-filling whichever side is missing. Useful for reconciliation — finding what is in one dataset and not the other.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a CROSS JOIN, and how do you write one by accident?
cards.a: Every combination of rows from both tables, with no condition. You write one by accident by listing two tables in FROM and forgetting the join predicate, producing a result set of size N×M.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a self join and when do you need one?
cards.a: Joining a table to itself with two aliases — for hierarchies (an employee's manager is another row in the same table) or for comparing rows to each other.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a lateral join?
cards.a: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true lets the subquery reference columns from the rows to its left. It is the clean way to write "for each row, the top 3 related rows."

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(col)?
cards.a: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col) counts rows where col is not null. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-null values.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does GROUP BY actually do?
cards.a: Collapses rows into one output row per distinct combination of the grouping expressions. Every selected column must either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is FILTER on an aggregate?
cards.a: A cleaner alternative to CASE inside an aggregate: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') counts only matching rows, letting you compute several conditional totals in one pass.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a scalar subquery?
cards.a: A subquery returning exactly one row and one column, usable anywhere a value is — WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products). It errors at runtime if it returns more than one row.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is a correlated subquery?
cards.a: A subquery referencing a column from the outer query, so it is conceptually re-evaluated per outer row. Postgres often rewrites these into joins, but they can be a performance trap when it cannot.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: IN versus EXISTS — what is the difference?
cards.a: EXISTS asks whether any matching row exists and can stop at the first hit; IN compares against a value list. They also differ on NULLs: NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows at all, which is a notorious silent bug. Prefer NOT EXISTS.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: Why is NOT IN (SELECT ...) dangerous?
cards.a: If the subquery returns even one NULL, every comparison becomes unknown and the whole predicate is never true, so the query returns zero rows with no error.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is UNION versus UNION ALL?
cards.a: UNION concatenates two result sets and removes duplicates, which requires a sort or hash. UNION ALL just concatenates. Use ALL unless you specifically need deduplication.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is DISTINCT ON?
cards.a: A Postgres extension: SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) * FROM events ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC returns the first row per user_id in the given order. A compact alternative to a window function for "latest per group."

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does ON CONFLICT do?
cards.a: Added in Postgres 9.5, it turns an INSERT into an upsert: ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name inserts or updates atomically, without a read-then-write race. DO NOTHING silently skips conflicts.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is EXCLUDED in an ON CONFLICT clause?
cards.a: A pseudo-table holding the row you tried to insert, so the update can reference the proposed values alongside the existing ones.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does RETURNING do?
cards.a: Returns rows affected by an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in the same round trip — most commonly INSERT ... RETURNING id to get a generated key without a second query.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is MERGE and how does it differ from ON CONFLICT?
cards.a: Added in Postgres 15, it is the SQL-standard statement for conditional insert/update/delete driven by a join against a source. It is more expressive than ON CONFLICT, which is keyed specifically on a unique constraint violation.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
cards.a: DELETE removes rows one at a time, is transactional, fires triggers, and leaves dead tuples. TRUNCATE discards the whole table's storage instantly, is still transactional in Postgres, but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and does not fire row triggers.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What does LIMIT ... OFFSET cost at large offsets?
cards.a: The server must still produce and discard every skipped row, so OFFSET 1000000 does a million rows of work to return ten. This is why deep pagination gets slower with page number.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is keyset (cursor) pagination?
cards.a: Paginating by a value rather than a count: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Constant time at any depth because the index can seek straight to the position.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: What is CASE used for in SQL?
cards.a: Conditional expressions inside a query — mapping values, bucketing, or conditional aggregation. CASE WHEN x > 100 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END.

cards.t: Node 3 · SQL is a question, not a program
cards.q: Why is SELECT * discouraged in application code?
cards.a: It fetches columns you do not need (including large TOASTed ones), it breaks silently when a column is added or reordered, and it prevents index-only scans. Name your columns.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is the heap?
cards.a: The file (or set of files) holding a table's row data. "Heap" means unordered pile: rows sit wherever there was room, in no meaningful order.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: How large is a Postgres page, and why does the number matter?
cards.a: 8192 bytes — 8 KB. It is a compile-time constant and effectively universal. It is the atom of all storage work: Postgres reads, writes and caches whole pages, so most performance numbers are really page counts.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is inside a page?
cards.a: A header, then a line pointer array growing down from the top, then row data growing up from the bottom, with free space in the middle.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is a tuple?
cards.a: Postgres's name for a stored row version. Each has a 23-byte header (padded to 24) before its column data; that header holds the transaction visibility information.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is a ctid?
cards.a: A row's physical address — a pair of (page number, line pointer). Visible via SELECT ctid, * FROM t. It is not stable: any update can move the row, so never store one.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: Why do heap files get split at 1 GB?
cards.a: Postgres splits each relation into segment files of 1 GB to stay within filesystem limits and keep file handling manageable. It is invisible in normal use.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: Why can't a row exceed 8 KB, and what saves you?
cards.a: A tuple cannot span pages. TOAST saves you: values that would push a row over roughly 2 KB are compressed and, if still too large, moved into a hidden side table in chunks, leaving a pointer in the main row.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What does TOAST stand for?
cards.a: The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is the practical performance consequence of TOAST?
cards.a: A column holding a megabyte of JSON costs almost nothing to SELECT unless you select that column. This is a concrete reason SELECT * on a wide table can be dramatically more expensive than naming four columns.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What are the TOAST storage strategies?
cards.a: PLAIN (no toasting), EXTENDED (compress then move out — the default for most variable-length types), EXTERNAL (move out without compressing, faster substring access), and MAIN (compress, avoid moving out if possible).

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: How does column order affect table size?
cards.a: Postgres aligns values on natural boundaries, so declaring bool, int8, bool, int8 wastes seven padding bytes after each boolean. Declaring fixed-width columns largest-first, then variable-length, then nullable, avoids it. Irrelevant on small tables, gigabytes on billions of rows.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is a sequential scan?
cards.a: Reading every page of a table and checking every row. It is one long streaming read, which disks handle well, so it is the fastest option for small tables and for queries matching a large fraction of rows.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: When does a sequential scan become catastrophic?
cards.a: When the table is large and the query is selective — a 50 GB table means 6.5 million page reads to find one row, repeated on every request.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is shared_buffers?
cards.a: Postgres's own cache of pages in memory, shared by all connections. Default 128 MB; conventionally set to about 25% of the machine's RAM.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: Why is Postgres caching described as double caching?
cards.a: Because underneath shared_buffers, the operating system keeps its own page cache of the same files. A page missing from shared_buffers is often still in RAM via the OS.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is effective_cache_size and what does it allocate?
cards.a: Nothing. It is a hint to the planner about how much total caching (Postgres plus OS) is likely available, which changes how cheap it thinks repeated index access will be. Typically set to 50–75% of RAM.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is fillfactor?
cards.a: The percentage of each page Postgres fills when inserting, default 100 for tables. Lowering it to around 90 leaves room for updated row versions on the same page, enabling HOT updates.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is the free space map?
cards.a: A per-relation structure recording how much usable space each page has, so inserts can reuse space reclaimed by VACUUM instead of always appending.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is the visibility map?
cards.a: A per-relation bitmap marking pages where all tuples are visible to all transactions. It is what makes index-only scans possible and what lets VACUUM skip pages entirely.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: How do you see how big a table is?
cards.a: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('t')) for table plus indexes plus TOAST, pg_relation_size('t') for the heap alone, and pg_indexes_size('t') for the indexes.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: Why does Postgres read a whole page to fetch one row?
cards.a: Because the page is the unit of I/O and of caching. There is no mechanism to read part of one, and in practice the neighbouring rows are often wanted next anyway.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is a relation?
cards.a: Postgres's internal term for anything table-shaped stored in files — tables, indexes, sequences, materialized views. It is why so many system functions and views are named *_relation_*.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: Does inserting a row put it anywhere meaningful in the heap?
cards.a: No. It goes wherever there is free space, which may be a hole left by a vacuumed dead tuple in the middle of the file. Physical order is not logical order.

cards.t: Node 4 · Pages, tuples and the heap
cards.q: What is physical correlation and why does it matter?
cards.a: How closely a column's ordering matches physical row order on disk. High correlation makes index scans cheap because matching rows cluster into few pages; it is why BRIN indexes work and why CLUSTER exists.

cards.q: What is an index?
cards.a: A separate data structure, in its own files, mapping values to the physical locations of the rows containing them — a redundant, automatically maintained copy of part of your data kept in an order that makes searching cheap.

cards.q: What are the two costs of an index?
cards.a: Disk space, and write amplification — every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update every index on the table. Ten indexes on a hot write table is a real problem.

cards.q: What structure does a default Postgres index use?
cards.a: A B+tree. Leaves hold every indexed value in sorted order paired with a ctid, and are linked to each other; internal pages hold separator keys.

cards.q: Why is a B-tree lookup so cheap?
cards.a: Each 8 KB page holds hundreds of keys, so fan-out is enormous. A hundred-million-row table typically has a tree only four levels deep, and the top levels stay cached — four page reads instead of millions.

cards.q: Which query shapes can a B-tree serve besides equality?
cards.a: Range queries (>, <, BETWEEN) because leaves are sorted and linked; ORDER BY on the indexed column, letting the sort be skipped; prefix matching LIKE 'abc%'; and MIN/MAX by reading one end.

cards.q: Why can't a B-tree help LIKE '%abc'?
cards.a: A suffix has no position in a value-sorted structure. Sorting by leading characters says nothing about trailing ones, so the whole index would have to be scanned.

cards.q: What does an index on (tenant_id, created_at) sort by?
cards.a: tenant_id first, and within equal tenant values, created_at. That is why it serves queries about one tenant well and queries about a date range across all tenants badly.

cards.q: State the leftmost prefix rule.
cards.a: A composite index is usable for a query that constrains a prefix of its columns. An index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a, on (a, b), and on (a, b, c) — not on b alone.

cards.q: What is the column ordering rule for a composite index?
cards.a: Equality columns first, then the range or sort column. Once you use a range predicate on a column, columns after it in the index can no longer be used for further seeking.

cards.q: What is a partial index and when does it pay off?
cards.a: CREATE INDEX ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL indexes only some rows. Where 98% of rows are soft-deleted or completed, the index becomes a fiftieth of the size and stays cached.

cards.q: What is an expression index and why is it necessary?
cards.a: CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)). A query filtering on lower(email) cannot use a plain index on email, because the index knows nothing about a function of the column. The function must be IMMUTABLE.

cards.q: What does INCLUDE do in a CREATE INDEX?
cards.a: Added in Postgres 11, it stores extra columns in the index leaves without making them part of the sort key. It exists to enable index-only scans without widening the searchable key.

cards.q: What is an index-only scan?
cards.a: A scan that answers the query entirely from the index without visiting the heap, possible when every column needed is in the index.

cards.q: Why does an index scan normally have to visit the heap at all?
cards.a: Because the index does not record visibility. An index entry points at a tuple, but only the tuple's header knows whether your transaction may see that version.

cards.q: If the index has all the columns, why might an index-only scan still hit the heap?
cards.a: Because it can only skip the heap for pages marked all-visible in the visibility map, which VACUUM maintains. Heap fetches in an index-only scan are a vacuum problem, not an index problem.

cards.q: What is a bitmap scan, and what problem does it solve?
cards.a: When many rows match, following the index one at a time produces random heap access. Postgres instead builds an in-memory bitmap of matching pages, sorts it, and reads those pages in physical order — Bitmap Index Scan feeding Bitmap Heap Scan.

cards.q: How can Postgres use two indexes for one query?
cards.a: By building a bitmap from each and combining them with AND or OR before reading the heap. This is why a bitmap plan can show BitmapAnd over two index scans.

cards.q: What is the "Recheck Cond" line in a bitmap heap scan?
cards.a: When the bitmap becomes lossy (it stores whole pages instead of individual rows because it ran out of work_mem), Postgres must recheck the condition on every row of those pages.

cards.q: What is a GIN index for?
cards.a: Values that contain many searchable items — array elements, JSONB keys and values, full-text search lexemes. It is an inverted index mapping each item to the rows containing it.

cards.q: What is a GiST index for?
cards.a: A framework for indexing things with overlap and containment rather than ordering: geometric shapes, ranges, nearest-neighbour search. PostGIS is built on it, and exclusion constraints require it.

cards.q: What is a BRIN index and when is it excellent?
cards.a: Block Range INdex: it stores only the min and max value for each group of pages, making it tiny. It is superb on append-only time-series tables where physical order already correlates with the indexed column, and useless when it does not.

cards.q: Why are hash indexes rarely used?
cards.a: They support only equality, offer little over a B-tree in practice, and were not even crash-safe before Postgres 10. A B-tree does everything they do plus ranges and ordering.

cards.q: What index types does pgvector add?
cards.a: IVFFlat, which clusters vectors into lists and searches the nearest few, and HNSW (pgvector 0.5.0, 2023), a graph index that is slower and larger to build but far better on the recall-versus-speed trade-off.

cards.q: Does Postgres index the referencing side of a foreign key automatically?
cards.a: No. It indexes the referenced primary key, which already had one. orders.customer_id gets nothing, so lookups by customer and deletes of parents both become sequential scans.

cards.q: You add an index and the query gets slower. Name three likely reasons.
cards.a: The planner is not using it and you added write cost for nothing; it is used but the query matches so many rows that random heap access beats a sequential scan; or statistics are stale and the planner chose it on a bad estimate.

cards.q: How do you find unused indexes?
cards.a: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0. An index with zero scans after a representative period of production is pure write and space overhead — subject to the caveat that the counters reset on restart and on replicas are separate.

cards.q: What is index bloat and why does it happen?
cards.a: Index pages accumulate dead entries and become sparsely filled as rows are updated and deleted, so the index grows larger than its data warrants. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) rebuilds it without blocking.

cards.q: What is B-tree deduplication?
cards.a: Added in Postgres 13, it stores a single copy of a repeated key with a list of pointers, dramatically shrinking indexes on low-cardinality columns.

cards.q: What does CREATE UNIQUE INDEX give you that a UNIQUE constraint does not?
cards.a: It can be partial — CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL enforces uniqueness only among live rows, which a declared constraint cannot express.

cards.q: Why is indexing a frequently-updated column more expensive than it looks?
cards.a: Because an update to an indexed column prevents the HOT optimisation, forcing new index entries in every index on the table rather than a cheap in-page chain.

cards.q: What is a covering index?
cards.a: One that contains every column a query needs, so the query can be answered by an index-only scan. Built either by adding columns to the key or, better, with INCLUDE.

cards.q: How selective must an index be to be worth using?
cards.a: There is no fixed number, but as a rule of thumb once a query matches more than roughly 5–10% of a table the planner will prefer a sequential scan, because random page access costs more than streaming.

cards.q: What is CLUSTER?
cards.a: A command that physically rewrites a table in the order of a chosen index, maximising correlation. It takes an exclusive lock and the order is not maintained afterwards, so it is a one-off, not a property.

cards.q: Can an index be used for ORDER BY ... DESC?
cards.a: Yes — B-tree leaves can be walked backwards. You only need an explicitly DESC index when mixing directions across columns, e.g. ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC.

cards.q: How do you index for a query that filters on one column and sorts by another?
cards.a: A composite index with the equality column first and the sort column second, so the index provides both the filter and the ordering and the sort node disappears from the plan.

cards.q: What is the trade-off of adding an index to speed up one report?
cards.a: Every write to that table pays for it forever, and it consumes cache space that other data could use. A report that runs hourly rarely justifies an index on a table written thousands of times per second.

cards.q: Why does a query on a small table ignore your index?
cards.a: Because reading the whole table is a handful of sequential pages and is genuinely cheaper than the index lookup plus heap fetch. The planner is right; the index will start being used as the table grows.

cards.q: What does pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_tup_fetch tell you?
cards.a: How many live rows were fetched via that index. Compared against idx_scan it tells you whether each use of the index returns one row or thousands.

cards.q: What does the planner do?
cards.a: It takes a parsed query, enumerates many possible execution strategies — which index or none, join order, join algorithm — assigns each a cost, and executes the cheapest.

cards.q: What are the units of planner cost?
cards.a: Abstract numbers, not milliseconds. They are built from constants where one sequential page read is defined as 1.0, a random page read defaults to 4.0, and processing one row is 0.01.

cards.q: What is random_page_cost and why change it?
cards.a: The estimated cost of a random page read, default 4.0 — calibrated for spinning disks. On SSDs it is conventionally lowered to about 1.1, and this single change is one of the highest-impact tuning steps because at 4.0 the planner systematically undervalues indexes.

cards.q: Where do the planner's row estimates come from?
cards.a: Column statistics in pg_statistic — the null fraction, the most common values with their frequencies, a histogram of the distribution, and the number of distinct values — gathered by ANALYZE.

cards.q: What runs ANALYZE in normal operation?
cards.a: Autovacuum, on its own threshold. This is why a table autovacuum cannot keep up with suffers both bloat and bad plans.

cards.q: What is the most common root cause of a catastrophically bad plan?
cards.a: A wrong row estimate. The planner thinks a step returns 5 rows, picks a nested loop, and the step actually returns 500,000.

cards.q: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
cards.a: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with estimates and does not run the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes it and annotates the plan with real timings and row counts.

cards.q: What is the danger of running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write statement?
cards.a: It really performs the write. Wrap it in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;.

cards.q: What is the single most valuable thing to look at in an EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
cards.a: The gap between rows= (estimate) and actual rows= on each line. A three-order-of-magnitude difference identifies exactly where the planner was misled.

cards.q: What does BUFFERS add to EXPLAIN?
cards.a: Counts of pages read, split into shared hit (found in shared_buffers) and shared read (fetched from the OS or disk), plus temp file usage. It turns "slow" into "read 400,000 pages."

cards.q: Which direction do you read an EXPLAIN plan?
cards.a: Inside out and bottom up — the most indented nodes execute first and feed their parents.

cards.q: Why can a node showing 0.02 ms actually account for forty seconds?
cards.a: Because timings and row counts on inner nodes are usually per loop. A node with actual time=0.02 rows=1 loops=200000 ran two hundred thousand times.

cards.q: Name the scan node types you must recognise.
cards.a: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Index Scan and Bitmap Heap Scan, plus Sort, Hash, Aggregate, Gather, Materialize and Memoize.

cards.q: How does a nested loop join work and when is it right?
cards.a: For each row on the outer side, look up matching rows on the inner side. Excellent when the outer side is tiny and the inner side is indexed; disastrous when the outer side turns out to be much larger than estimated.

cards.q: How does a hash join work and when is it right?
cards.a: Build a hash table of the smaller side in memory, then stream the larger side past it. The workhorse for joining two large tables on equality. It needs enough work_mem or it spills to disk in batches.

cards.q: How does a merge join work and when is it right?
cards.a: Both sides are sorted on the join key and walked together like merging two sorted lists. Good when indexes already provide the ordering so the sorts are free.

cards.q: What is work_mem, precisely?
cards.a: The memory allowed per sort or hash operation, default 4 MB. Not per query, not per server. One query can have several such operations, and many connections run them at once.

cards.q: What is the worst-case memory formula for work_mem?
cards.a: Roughly work_mem × operations per query × concurrent connections. This is why raising it globally to 1 GB on a 100-connection server is how machines run out of memory.

cards.q: How do you know a sort spilled to disk?
cards.a: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk: 24000kB instead of quicksort Memory: .... Enable log_temp_files to catch it in production.

cards.q: Does Postgres support query hints?
cards.a: No, deliberately. The project's position is that hints become permanently wrong as data changes. The escape hatches are enable_* settings for diagnosis, CREATE STATISTICS, and raising the statistics target.

cards.q: What is CREATE STATISTICS for?
cards.a: Telling the planner about correlations between columns it otherwise assumes are independent — e.g. city and postcode. Without it the planner multiplies selectivities and underestimates dramatically.

cards.q: What is default_statistics_target?
cards.a: How many histogram buckets and most-common-values entries ANALYZE collects, default 100. Raising it per column (ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 1000) helps on heavily skewed data at the cost of slower ANALYZE.

cards.q: When did Postgres gain parallel query, and what does it look like in a plan?
cards.a: Postgres 9.6. Plans show a Gather node above parallel-aware scans or joins, and row counts beneath it are per worker.

cards.q: What controls how many parallel workers a query gets?
cards.a: max_parallel_workers_per_gather (per node), max_parallel_workers and max_worker_processes (server-wide), plus table size thresholds — small tables never go parallel.

cards.q: What is a generic plan versus a custom plan?
cards.a: For prepared statements, Postgres first builds custom plans using the actual parameter values; after five executions it may switch to a parameter-independent generic plan. On skewed data the generic plan can be much worse. Controlled by plan_cache_mode.

cards.q: What is a Memoize node?
cards.a: Added in Postgres 14, it caches inner-side results in a nested loop so repeated lookups of the same key are not re-executed. It turns some bad nested loops into good ones.

cards.q: What does SET enable_seqscan = off actually do?
cards.a: It does not forbid sequential scans; it adds a huge cost penalty so the planner avoids them if any alternative exists. It is a diagnostic tool for confirming an index would help, not a production setting.

cards.q: A query is fast in psql and slow from the application. What are the likely causes?
cards.a: A generic plan chosen for a prepared statement, different session settings (work_mem, search_path), different parameter values or types causing a cast that defeats an index, or the application fetching far more rows than you tested with.

cards.q: What does ANALYZE tablename do, as a command?
cards.a: Samples the table and refreshes its statistics immediately. It is the first thing to run after a bulk load or a large data change, because the planner is otherwise working from the previous shape of the data.

cards.q: How do you get a plan in a machine-readable form?
cards.a: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) SELECT ... — which is what visualisation tools consume.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is a transaction?
cards.a: A group of statements that either all take effect or none do. BEGIN opens one, COMMIT makes it permanent, ROLLBACK discards it, and a dropped connection or crash acts as a rollback.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: Is a single statement outside BEGIN in a transaction?
cards.a: Yes. Postgres wraps every standalone statement in its own transaction — this is autocommit, the default in psql and in every driver.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What does the A in ACID prevent?
cards.a: Atomicity — all or nothing, so money never disappears between two updates and no half-completed multi-step change is ever visible or persisted.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What does the C in ACID mean in Postgres?
cards.a: Consistency — declared constraints hold at commit, so no transaction can leave a foreign key dangling or a check violated.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What does the D in ACID require mechanically?
cards.a: Durability — once COMMIT returns, the change survives immediate power loss. Since writing to a file does not put bytes on disk, this needs an explicit flush.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is the WAL and what is the rule in its name?
cards.a: The Write-Ahead Log. Before any change to a data page may reach disk, a record describing that change must be written to the log and physically flushed.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What happens mechanically when you COMMIT?
cards.a: Postgres writes a commit record to the WAL and calls fsync, which does not return until the bytes are on physical media. Only then does it report success. The modified data pages are still dirty in shared_buffers.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: Why is the WAL faster than writing data pages directly?
cards.a: Because it is a strictly sequential append to one file, which storage handles far better than scattered random writes across a large table. Every commit becomes one append.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is a checkpoint?
cards.a: A periodic operation that flushes all dirty pages to their data files and records that everything before this point is safely on disk, so recovery need only replay WAL from there forward.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What happens during crash recovery?
cards.a: Postgres replays the WAL from the last checkpoint, redoing every logged change not yet written to its data page. Because replay is deterministic and idempotent, the database returns to exactly the last successful commit.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: Someone says "Postgres crashed and we lost committed data." What is almost certainly true?
cards.a: A configuration or hardware problem — fsync = off, synchronous_commit = off, or storage that lies about having flushed. The WAL design does not permit losing an acknowledged commit on honest hardware.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What does synchronous_commit = off trade away?
cards.a: Commits return before the WAL is flushed, so up to a fraction of a second of committed transactions can be lost in a crash. The database stays consistent — this is not corruption — so it is often a good trade for a background job queue and a bad one for payments.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is full_page_writes and why does WAL volume spike after a checkpoint?
cards.a: A power failure can tear an 8 KB page mid-write, so the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs the entire page image. That is why WAL generation jumps immediately after every checkpoint.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: Why is the WAL the foundation of replication and PITR?
cards.a: Because it is a complete description of every change. Shipping it to another machine and replaying it produces an identical copy; stopping the replay at a chosen point reproduces the database as of that moment.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is transactional DDL and why is it a Postgres advantage?
cards.a: CREATE, ALTER and DROP participate in transactions and roll back cleanly. Oracle and MySQL cannot do this. It means a failed migration leaves nothing half-applied.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is a savepoint?
cards.a: A named point inside a transaction — SAVEPOINT s1 — that you can ROLLBACK TO without aborting the whole transaction. Drivers and ORMs implement nested transactions with these.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: In Postgres, what happens to a transaction after any error?
cards.a: It enters an aborted state and rejects every further statement with "current transaction is aborted" until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint). Unlike some databases, you cannot simply continue.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is a two-phase commit / prepared transaction?
cards.a: PREPARE TRANSACTION 'id' persists a transaction in a ready-to-commit state so an external coordinator can commit it across systems. Dangerous operationally: a forgotten prepared transaction holds locks and blocks vacuum forever.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What are WAL segments and where do they live?
cards.a: Fixed-size files (16 MB by default) in the pg_wal/ directory, written sequentially and recycled once no longer needed for recovery, replication, or archiving.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is wal_level?
cards.a: How much information is written to the WAL: minimal, replica (the default, enough for physical replication and archiving), or logical (enough to decode row-level changes for logical replication).

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What limits how much WAL accumulates?
cards.a: max_wal_size triggers checkpoints; wal_keep_size and replication slots keep segments around for standbys; archiving keeps them until archive_command succeeds. A failing archive command or an abandoned replication slot fills the disk.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is pg_wal filling up usually caused by?
cards.a: An inactive replication slot holding segments for a standby that no longer exists, or a failing archive_command. Never delete WAL files by hand.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: Why is a rollback in Postgres instantaneous?
cards.a: Because nothing needs undoing — the transaction's row versions are simply never made visible. Marking the transaction aborted is the entire operation. The dead versions are cleaned up later by VACUUM.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is checkpoint_completion_target?
cards.a: The fraction of the interval over which a checkpoint spreads its writes, default 0.9. Spreading them avoids an I/O spike that stalls queries.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What is the background writer?
cards.a: A process that trickles dirty pages out of shared_buffers ahead of checkpoints so that backends rarely have to write a page themselves in order to find a free buffer.

cards.t: Node 7 · Transactions, the WAL and durability
cards.q: What does xact_commit and xact_rollback in pg_stat_database tell you?
cards.a: The commit and rollback counts for the database. A high or rising rollback ratio usually means application errors or serialization failures, not deliberate rollbacks.

cards.q: What does MVCC stand for and what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Multi-Version Concurrency Control. It lets many transactions read and write concurrently without readers taking locks, avoiding the situation where one long report blocks all writes.

cards.q: State the headline property of MVCC in one sentence.
cards.a: Readers never block writers and writers never block readers; only two writers touching the same row block each other.

cards.q: What are xmin and xmax?
cards.a: Fields in every tuple's header. xmin is the id of the transaction that created this version; xmax is the id of the transaction that deleted or superseded it, or zero if it is still live.

cards.q: How can you actually see them?
cards.a: SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts; — they are hidden system columns available on every table.

cards.q: What does an UPDATE physically do in Postgres?
cards.a: It writes an entirely new tuple with the new values and the current transaction as its xmin, and sets xmax on the old tuple. Both versions exist in the heap simultaneously. It does not modify the row in place.

cards.q: What does a DELETE physically do?
cards.a: Sets xmax on the existing tuple. Nothing new is written and nothing is removed at that moment.

cards.q: What is a snapshot?
cards.a: The set of transactions that had committed at the instant the snapshot was taken. A transaction judges every tuple's visibility against its snapshot.

cards.q: State the visibility rule in plain terms.
cards.a: A tuple version is visible to you if the transaction that created it had committed as of your snapshot, and the transaction that deleted it either does not exist or had not committed as of your snapshot.

cards.q: Why is SELECT count(*) slow on a large Postgres table?
cards.a: Because how many rows exist depends on who is asking. There is no maintained counter to read; every row's visibility must be evaluated, so the table (or a covering index) must be scanned.

cards.q: How do you get a fast approximate row count?
cards.a: SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 't'. It is the planner's estimate, updated by ANALYZE, and is usually close enough for a dashboard.

cards.q: Why must an index scan visit the heap to check visibility?
cards.a: Because the index entry records only the value and the ctid. Visibility lives in the tuple header, so only the heap tuple can say whether your transaction may see that version.

cards.q: What is a HOT update?
cards.a: A Heap-Only Tuple update, from Postgres 8.3: if the update changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same page, the versions are chained within the page and no index is touched at all.

cards.q: How does fillfactor relate to HOT updates?
cards.a: HOT requires free space on the same page. Lowering fillfactor to around 90 on a heavily-updated table reserves that space, raising the fraction of updates that can be HOT.

cards.q: How is Postgres's MVCC different from Oracle's or InnoDB's?
cards.a: They update rows in place and keep old versions in a separate undo log. Postgres keeps every version in the table itself, which makes rollback instant and reads simple — and creates bloat, which they do not have.

cards.q: What is the cost side of Postgres's MVCC choice?
cards.a: Every update leaves a dead tuple in the table and stale entries in every index, so the table grows even when the row count does not, and something must clean up afterwards.

cards.q: What is txid_current() / pg_current_xact_id()?
cards.a: A function returning the current transaction's id. Useful for demonstrating xmin behaviour and for reasoning about visibility while learning.

cards.q: Do read-only transactions consume a transaction id?
cards.a: Not a permanent one — Postgres assigns a real xid lazily, only when a transaction first writes. Read-only transactions get a virtual id, which is why a read-heavy workload does not burn through the xid space.

cards.q: What is the "snapshot too old" idea?
cards.a: A configurable limit after which a very long-running transaction's snapshot is invalidated so vacuum can proceed. It trades an error in that transaction for the ability to reclaim space.

cards.q: How does MVCC interact with sequences?
cards.a: It does not — sequences deliberately live outside transactional visibility, which is why nextval is never rolled back and identity columns have gaps.

cards.q: Why does a long-running SELECT not block a concurrent UPDATE?
cards.a: The updater appends a new row version rather than modifying the one the reader is looking at, and the reader's snapshot keeps pointing at the old version, which still physically exists.

cards.q: Two transactions update the same row concurrently under MVCC. What happens?
cards.a: The second one blocks on the first one's row lock until it commits or rolls back, then proceeds (re-evaluating its WHERE clause under READ COMMITTED). MVCC removes locking from reads, not from writes.

cards.q: What determines whether a dead tuple can actually be removed?
cards.a: Whether any still-running transaction could see it. The oldest running transaction's snapshot defines the horizon, and nothing newer than that horizon can be cleaned up.

cards.q: When is a tuple dead?
cards.a: When no running transaction could possibly still need to see it — its deleting transaction committed before the oldest active snapshot.

cards.q: What are the three costs of dead tuples?
cards.a: They occupy disk, they occupy shared_buffers when their page is read, and every scan reads past them.

cards.q: What is bloat?
cards.a: A table or index whose physical size is far larger than the live data it holds. It is the most common reason a database that was fast six months ago is slow now with the same amount of data.

cards.q: What does plain VACUUM do?
cards.a: Scans the table, removes dead tuples' index entries, marks their space reusable in the free space map, and updates the visibility map. It runs concurrently with normal traffic and takes no exclusive lock.

cards.q: Does plain VACUUM shrink the file?
cards.a: No. Space is marked reusable within the existing file. Only if dead space is at the very end can the file be truncated.

cards.q: What does VACUUM FULL do and why is it dangerous?
cards.a: It rewrites the whole table into a new file, genuinely returning disk to the OS, while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks even SELECT. On a large table that is hours of total outage.

cards.q: What is the online alternative to VACUUM FULL?
cards.a: The pg_repack extension, which rebuilds a table or index without a long exclusive lock, taking a brief one only at the swap.

cards.q: What is autovacuum?
cards.a: A background daemon that watches per-table statistics and triggers VACUUM and ANALYZE when dead tuple or change counts cross thresholds.

cards.q: What is the default autovacuum trigger formula?
cards.a: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) plus autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) × estimated row count. So a table is vacuumed after roughly 20% of it has churned.

cards.q: Why is the 0.2 scale factor wrong on large tables?
cards.a: On a hundred-million-row table it means waiting for twenty million dead tuples before cleanup starts. The standard fix is a per-table override: ALTER TABLE t SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01).

cards.q: What single thing most commonly defeats autovacuum?
cards.a: A connection sitting idle in transaction. It pins the visibility horizon database-wide, so nothing newer than that transaction can be cleaned anywhere.

cards.q: Besides idle transactions, what else holds back the vacuum horizon?
cards.a: Long-running queries, abandoned prepared (two-phase) transactions, inactive replication slots, and standbys with hot_standby_feedback = on.

cards.q: You see autovacuum running constantly on a growing table and reclaiming nothing. What do you check first?
cards.a: SELECT pid, state, xact_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start; — find the oldest transaction pinning the horizon.

cards.q: What is transaction id wraparound?
cards.a: The xid is a 32-bit counter, so it wraps after about 4 billion transactions. Since visibility is decided by comparing xids, a wrap would make ancient rows look like they came from the future and become invisible — silent total data loss.

cards.q: How does Postgres prevent wraparound?
cards.a: By freezing: vacuum marks sufficiently old tuples as committed-and-visible-to-everyone, removing them from xid comparison entirely.

cards.q: What is autovacuum_freeze_max_age?
cards.a: Default 200 million. Once a table's oldest unfrozen xid is that old, an anti-wraparound vacuum is forced even on tables autovacuum would otherwise skip, and it cannot be cancelled.

cards.q: What happens if freezing falls far enough behind?
cards.a: Postgres begins warning, then refuses writes to protect itself, and the only cure is a vacuum that must now run in single-user mode. This has taken down real companies.

cards.q: How do you monitor wraparound risk?
cards.a: Watch age(datfrozenxid) per database and age(relfrozenxid) per table against autovacuum_freeze_max_age.

cards.q: What is maintenance_work_mem and why does it matter to vacuum?
cards.a: The memory a maintenance operation may use, default 64 MB. Vacuum stores dead tuple identifiers in it; if it fills, vacuum must make multiple passes over every index. Raising it to hundreds of megabytes or 1 GB dramatically speeds vacuum on big tables.

cards.q: What are autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and cost_limit?
cards.a: Throttles that pause autovacuum after a budget of page accesses so it does not saturate I/O. On modern hardware the defaults are often far too conservative and are why autovacuum cannot keep up.

cards.q: How do you see when a table was last vacuumed?
cards.a: SELECT relname, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

cards.q: Why is a table of 10 million rows that you update constantly worse than one you only insert into?
cards.a: Every update creates a dead tuple, so an update-heavy table generates cleanup work proportional to its write rate, while an insert-only table generates almost none.

cards.q: Does VACUUM help query plans?
cards.a: Indirectly and directly: it updates the visibility map (enabling index-only scans) and autovacuum also runs ANALYZE, which refreshes the statistics the planner depends on.

cards.q: What is VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) tablename useful for?
cards.a: Running both operations on demand and printing exactly how many tuples were removed, how many could not be removed yet, and how many pages were skipped — the fastest way to confirm a horizon problem.

cards.q: What is an isolation level?
cards.a: The dial controlling how strongly concurrent transactions are separated from each other — specifically, which anomalies they are permitted to experience.

cards.q: Which isolation levels does Postgres actually implement?
cards.a: Three distinct behaviours: READ COMMITTED (the default), REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted but behaves as READ COMMITTED, because MVCC makes dirty reads impossible.

cards.q: What is a dirty read, and can it happen in Postgres?
cards.a: Seeing another transaction's uncommitted change. It cannot happen in Postgres at any isolation level.

cards.q: What is a non-repeatable read?
cards.a: Running the same SELECT twice in one transaction and getting different values, because another transaction committed a change in between.

cards.q: What is a phantom read?
cards.a: Running the same range query twice in one transaction and finding rows that were not there before, because another transaction inserted them.

cards.q: What is a lost update?
cards.a: Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new one from it, and the second write overwrites the first. Available at READ COMMITTED.

cards.q: What is write skew?
cards.a: Two transactions read overlapping data, each verifies an invariant that currently holds, and each writes something individually fine that together breaks the invariant — e.g. two on-call doctors each cancelling after checking that someone else is on call.

cards.q: What defines READ COMMITTED in Postgres?
cards.a: The snapshot is taken per statement. Each statement sees everything committed before it started, so two identical SELECTs in one transaction can legitimately differ.

cards.q: What anomalies does READ COMMITTED permit?
cards.a: Non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates and write skew. It prevents only dirty reads.

cards.q: What is the EPQ re-check under READ COMMITTED?
cards.a: If an UPDATE reaches a row another transaction is concurrently updating, it blocks, waits for that transaction to commit, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the new version and proceeds only if it still matches.

cards.q: Why does the EPQ re-check surprise people?
cards.a: Because UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending' can act on a row that was pending when the statement began but is not any more, or skip one it appeared to select. Under a single statement the read and the write are not against the same snapshot.

cards.q: What defines REPEATABLE READ in Postgres?
cards.a: One snapshot taken at the first statement and held for the whole transaction, so every read is consistent with every other. Non-repeatable reads and phantoms are eliminated.

cards.q: Why is Postgres's REPEATABLE READ stronger than the SQL standard requires?
cards.a: The standard allows phantoms at that level; Postgres's implementation is snapshot isolation, which prevents them.

cards.q: What new failure does REPEATABLE READ introduce?
cards.a: Updating a row modified after your snapshot raises ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update, SQLSTATE 40001, and aborts the transaction. Your application must retry.

cards.q: What does SERIALIZABLE guarantee?
cards.a: That the outcome is identical to some serial order of running the concurrent transactions one after another. Every anomaly, including write skew, is eliminated.

cards.q: How does Postgres implement SERIALIZABLE?
cards.a: With SSI, Serializable Snapshot Isolation, added in 9.1. It tracks read/write dependencies between concurrent transactions and aborts one when it detects a dependency cycle that could not occur in any serial order.

cards.q: Is SERIALIZABLE pessimistic or optimistic in Postgres?
cards.a: Optimistic — it does not block; it detects and aborts. So it costs you retries under contention rather than waiting.

cards.q: What must application code do to use REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE safely?
cards.a: Wrap transactions in a retry loop that catches SQLSTATE 40001 (and 40P01 for deadlocks) and re-runs the whole transaction with backoff. This is a contract, not an edge case.

cards.q: How do you set the isolation level?
cards.a: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; or SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ... as the first statement, or globally via default_transaction_isolation.

cards.q: Which isolation level should a typical web application use?
cards.a: READ COMMITTED, the default — and close specific races explicitly with SELECT FOR UPDATE, unique constraints, or atomic statements, rather than by raising the level globally.

cards.q: When is REPEATABLE READ the right choice?
cards.a: For reports and exports that must be internally consistent across many queries — every part of the output reflects the same instant.

cards.q: When is SERIALIZABLE worth it?
cards.a: When an invariant spans multiple rows or tables and you would rather pay in occasional retries than reason about every possible interleaving in application code.

cards.q: Does a higher isolation level make a single statement safer?
cards.a: A single statement is already atomic and sees one snapshot. Isolation levels matter when a transaction spans multiple statements, or when it reads and then writes based on what it read.

cards.q: What is the cheapest way to prevent a lost update without changing isolation level?
cards.a: Make the update self-contained — UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 reads and writes atomically inside one statement, so no interleaving is possible.

cards.q: Where are row-level locks stored in Postgres?
cards.a: In the tuple itself, in the xmax field — not in a lock table. That is why locking a million rows costs no extra memory and there is no limit on how many rows you can lock.

cards.q: What does SELECT ... FOR UPDATE do?
cards.a: Locks the returned rows as if you were about to update them, so no other transaction can modify them until yours ends. It is how you close a lost-update race: read with FOR UPDATE, compute, write, commit.

cards.q: What is the difference between FOR UPDATE and FOR NO KEY UPDATE?
cards.a: FOR NO KEY UPDATE is weaker and is what a plain UPDATE of non-key columns takes; it does not conflict with FOR KEY SHARE, which is what foreign-key checks take. Using the weaker mode reduces contention with child-row inserts.

cards.q: What are FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE?
cards.a: Shared row locks: multiple transactions may hold them simultaneously, but writers are blocked. FOR KEY SHARE is the weakest, taken automatically to protect a row referenced by a foreign key.

cards.q: What does SKIP LOCKED do and what is it for?
cards.a: Added in 9.5, it makes a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE silently skip rows another transaction has locked. It is how you build a job queue on a table: each worker claims the next N unlocked pending jobs with no contention and no double processing.

cards.q: What does NOWAIT do?
cards.a: Raises an error immediately instead of waiting if a requested row lock is unavailable — useful when you would rather fail fast than queue.

cards.q: Sketch the SQL for claiming a job from a queue table.
cards.a: UPDATE jobs SET status='running' WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10) RETURNING *;

cards.q: What table-level lock does a plain SELECT take?
cards.a: ACCESS SHARE, the weakest mode, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

cards.q: What lock does an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE take on the table?
cards.a: ROW EXCLUSIVE. It is compatible with ACCESS SHARE and with itself, which is why ordinary traffic never blocks ordinary traffic at the table level.

cards.q: What takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and what does it conflict with?
cards.a: Most ALTER TABLE forms, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, REINDEX. It conflicts with everything, including plain SELECT.

cards.q: Explain how one ALTER TABLE takes down a healthy site.
cards.a: The ALTER must acquire ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and cannot while any transaction holds any lock on the table. It queues behind a slow SELECT — and because lock requests are granted in order, every subsequent query queues behind the ALTER. Thousands of queries pile up and the ALTER never even runs.

cards.q: What is the standard mitigation for that?
cards.a: Set lock_timeout (e.g. SET lock_timeout = '3s') before DDL so it gives up rather than queueing, and retry. Never run unbounded DDL against a busy table.

cards.q: What is a deadlock?
cards.a: Transaction A holds a lock B wants while B holds a lock A wants. Neither can proceed.

cards.q: How does Postgres handle deadlocks?
cards.a: After deadlock_timeout (default 1 second) it runs cycle detection on the wait graph and aborts one transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected, SQLSTATE 40P01.

cards.q: What causes most application deadlocks?
cards.a: Updating multiple rows in an order determined by a hash map or set iteration, so two concurrent requests touch the same rows in different orders.

cards.q: What is the standard fix for application deadlocks?
cards.a: Establish a consistent lock ordering — ORDER BY id before locking, or always touch tables in the same sequence — plus a retry on 40P01.

cards.q: What are advisory locks?
cards.a: Application-defined locks unrelated to any row: pg_advisory_lock(key) (session-scoped) and pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) (released at commit). They give you a distributed mutex without adding infrastructure.

cards.q: What is a typical use of an advisory lock?
cards.a: Ensuring only one instance of a scheduled job runs across all application servers, or serialising an expensive rebuild without locking the underlying table.

cards.q: Why must session-scoped advisory locks be avoided behind PgBouncer transaction pooling?
cards.a: Because the connection you hold the lock on is returned to the pool between statements, so your next statement may run on a different backend that does not hold it.

cards.q: How do you find what is blocking a query?
cards.a: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0; — it gives the blocking chain directly.

cards.q: How do you cancel or kill a problem query?
cards.a: pg_cancel_backend(pid) cancels the running query and leaves the connection; pg_terminate_backend(pid) kills the whole connection. Try cancel first.

cards.q: What is lock_timeout versus statement_timeout?
cards.a: lock_timeout caps how long a statement waits to acquire a lock; statement_timeout caps total statement runtime including execution.

cards.q: Which ALTER TABLE forms take a weaker lock than ACCESS EXCLUSIVE?
cards.a: A number of them since Postgres 9.4–13, including ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT and SET STATISTICS. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which permits reads and writes.

cards.q: Why can two transactions inserting different rows into the same table never block each other?
