cards.a: Both take only ROW EXCLUSIVE on the table, which is self-compatible, and they lock different tuples. They collide only if they insert the same value into a unique index.

cards.q: What is Postgres's connection model?
cards.a: Process per connection. The postmaster listens on 5432 and forks a dedicated operating-system process for each client, for the lifetime of that connection. Not a thread — a full process.

cards.q: Why did Postgres choose processes over threads, and is it still true in version 18?
cards.a: Process isolation means a crash in one backend cannot corrupt another, and it kept the code much simpler for decades. It is still the model in Postgres 18.

cards.q: What does each connection cost?
cards.a: A few megabytes of private memory before it does any work, an entry in the OS scheduler, and single-digit milliseconds to fork — enormous next to a 0.2 ms query.

cards.q: Why does throughput fall as connections rise past a point?
cards.a: More backends means more context switching and more contention on shared memory structures. Past roughly a small multiple of the CPU core count, adding connections reduces total throughput.

cards.q: What is the default max_connections?
cards.a: 100. Raising it to thousands to "handle more load" is one of the most reliable ways to make a database slower.

cards.q: What is a connection pool?
cards.a: A fixed set of connections opened once and handed out to requests, returned when each finishes — so the fork cost is paid once and the number of backends stays bounded.

cards.q: What are the important settings on pg.Pool in Node?
cards.a: max (how many connections — typically 10–20 per app instance, far fewer than people expect), idleTimeoutMillis, and connectionTimeoutMillis.

cards.q: Why do teams hit "too many clients already" despite using a pool?
cards.a: Because max is per process. 20 × 4 Node instances × 3 containers is 240 connections against a max_connections of 100.

cards.q: What is PgBouncer?
cards.a: An external connection pooler sitting between applications and Postgres, accepting thousands of client connections and multiplexing them onto a small number of real backends.

cards.q: What is session pooling?
cards.a: A real backend is assigned to a client for the whole connection. Safe, preserves all session state, and gives almost no benefit over no pooler.

cards.q: What is transaction pooling and why is it the default at serverless providers?
cards.a: A backend is assigned only for the duration of a transaction and returned at commit, so a handful of backends serve thousands of clients. It is where the large win is.

cards.q: What breaks under transaction pooling?
cards.a: Anything carrying session state: persistent SET, session-level advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, cursors held across statements, temporary tables, and server-side prepared statements.

cards.q: How do drivers and ORMs cope with transaction pooling?
cards.a: With an explicit flag disabling server-side prepared statements — prepare: false in postgres.js, ?pgbouncer=true in Prisma's connection string. Without it you get "prepared statement already exists" errors under load.

cards.q: What is statement pooling?
cards.a: The strictest mode: a backend is returned after every single statement, which forbids multi-statement transactions entirely. Rarely usable.

cards.q: What is a prepared statement?
cards.a: A parameterised query template Postgres parses and plans once, then executes repeatedly with different values, saving parse and plan time.

cards.q: Why are prepared statements the correct defence against SQL injection?
cards.a: Because parameters are sent separately from the query text and are never parsed as SQL. The query structure is fixed before any user value is involved, so no value can become syntax.

cards.q: What is the one thing parameters cannot do?
cards.a: Parameterise identifiers — table names, column names, sort direction. Dynamic ORDER BY must be validated against an allow-list, never interpolated.

cards.q: What is statement_timeout and why set it?
cards.a: A cap on how long any statement may run. Without it a runaway query holds locks and pins the vacuum horizon indefinitely. Setting it per role or per application is basic hygiene.

cards.q: What is idle_in_transaction_session_timeout?
cards.a: A cap on how long a connection may sit inside an open transaction doing nothing before Postgres terminates it. It is the direct defence against the autovacuum problem from Node 9.

cards.q: Why is opening a connection per HTTP request catastrophic in Node?
cards.a: Every request pays the fork and authentication cost, and under any concurrency you exceed max_connections immediately. The pool must live at module scope, created once.

cards.q: What is the rough formula for sizing a pool?
cards.a: Small. A common starting point is a few times the number of database CPU cores in total across all app instances, not per instance — often far fewer than the number of concurrent requests, because queries are short.

cards.q: What happens when every pooled connection is busy?
cards.a: New requests queue in the pool. If the pool has no timeout they wait forever and the application appears frozen, with nothing wrong visible on the database side.

cards.q: What do RDS Proxy, Supavisor and Neon's pooler have in common with PgBouncer?
cards.a: They are all transaction-mode poolers solving the same problem, and they carry the same restrictions on session state and prepared statements.

cards.q: Why do serverless platforms make connection pooling harder?
cards.a: Because each function instance is a separate process with its own pool and an unpredictable lifetime, so the total connection count scales with concurrency rather than with the number of servers. An external pooler becomes mandatory.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What is a migration?
cards.a: A versioned, checked-in script that moves the schema from one state to the next, applied in order, exactly once, tracked in a table the migration tool owns — so the schema is reproducible from an empty database.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What does transactional DDL give a migration tool?
cards.a: The ability to wrap each migration in a transaction, guaranteeing it is all-or-nothing. A failed migration leaves nothing half-applied, unlike MySQL where you clean up by hand.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Which schema changes are catalog-only and effectively instant?
cards.a: Adding a nullable column; adding a column with a constant default (Postgres 11+); dropping a column; renaming anything; widening varchar(50) to varchar(100) or to text.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Why is adding a column with a constant default now cheap?
cards.a: Postgres 11 stores the default in the catalog and materialises it lazily when rows are next written, instead of rewriting every row. This removed one of the most notorious causes of migration downtime.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Which schema changes rewrite the whole table?
cards.a: Adding a column with a volatile default such as gen_random_uuid(); changing a column type in a way that changes its storage representation, e.g. integer to bigint.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Which changes scan the table under a strong lock without rewriting it?
cards.a: Adding NOT NULL to an existing column, and adding a CHECK or foreign key constraint — each must verify every existing row.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What does dropping a column actually do?
cards.a: Marks it dropped in the catalog and stops showing it. The bytes stay in the tuples until rows are rewritten, so the table does not shrink immediately.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What is CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
cards.a: An index build that does not block reads or writes, achieved by scanning the table twice and tracking concurrent changes. It takes longer and takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What are the two caveats of CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
cards.a: It cannot run inside a transaction block, so your migration tool must be told not to wrap it; and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index behind that you must drop and retry.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: How do you find an invalid index?
cards.a: SELECT * FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid; — then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and rebuild.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What does ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID do?
cards.a: Adds the constraint so it is enforced on all new and modified rows, taking only a brief lock and scanning nothing. Existing rows are not checked.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What does VALIDATE CONSTRAINT do afterwards?
cards.a: Scans the existing rows to confirm they satisfy the constraint, under a lock weak enough to permit concurrent reads and writes. This two-step is how you add constraints to a large live table safely.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: How do you add NOT NULL to a huge table without a long lock?
cards.a: Add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE it, then (Postgres 12+) SET NOT NULL, which is instant because the planner can prove it from the validated check. Finally drop the redundant check.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What is the expand–migrate–contract pattern?
cards.a: Add the new structure alongside the old; deploy code writing to both and reading the old; backfill in batches; deploy code reading the new; drop the old in a later release. Every step is independently reversible.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Why must a backfill be batched?
cards.a: One giant UPDATE creates a dead tuple per row, generates enormous WAL, holds locks for the duration, and cannot be interrupted safely. Batches with a commit between each keep every unit small.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What does a batched backfill loop look like?
cards.a: Repeatedly UPDATE t SET new = f(old) WHERE new IS NULL AND id IN (SELECT id FROM t WHERE new IS NULL LIMIT 5000), committing between iterations, until zero rows are affected.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Why does a rolling deploy constrain what a migration may do?
cards.a: Because old and new application code run simultaneously against the same database. The schema must be compatible with both — which is exactly why you never rename or drop in the same release that introduces the replacement.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What must always be set in a migration that takes a strong lock?
cards.a: lock_timeout, so the DDL fails fast rather than queueing every subsequent query behind it.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Why is renaming a column dangerous even though it is instant?
cards.a: Because the old application code, still running during the deploy, refers to the old name and immediately errors. Use expand–migrate–contract instead.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: How should a migration tool handle CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
cards.a: By running that migration outside a transaction. Most tools have an explicit escape hatch for this; ignoring it produces "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block".

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What is the safest way to change a column's type?
cards.a: Add a new column of the target type, backfill in batches, switch reads and writes, then drop the old one — rather than ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a large table.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Should migrations contain data changes as well as schema changes?
cards.a: Small, deterministic data fixes are fine. Large backfills belong in a separate, resumable, batched job, because a migration that runs for an hour blocks your deploy pipeline and cannot be safely retried.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: What is a down migration and is it always worth writing?
cards.a: The reverse of a migration. It is worth writing while the change is still additive; once you have dropped a column the down migration cannot restore data, so the honest answer is that reversibility comes from ordering (expand–contract), not from down scripts.

cards.t: Node 13 · Migrations on a live schema
cards.q: Why check migrations into the repository rather than applying changes by hand?
cards.a: Because the schema is part of the application's definition. Hand-applied changes cannot be reviewed, reproduced in another environment, or replayed onto a fresh database.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is the difference between json and jsonb?
cards.a: json stores the text verbatim — whitespace, key order and duplicate keys preserved — and reparses on every access. jsonb parses once into a decomposed binary form, losing key order and duplicates but making access fast and, decisively, making it indexable.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: Which should you use by default?
cards.a: jsonb, unless you specifically need to preserve the exact original document text.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What do -> and ->> do?
cards.a: -> extracts a JSON value (still JSON); ->> extracts it as text. #> and #>> follow a path array.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What does the @> operator ask?
cards.a: Containment — does this JSONB document contain the given structure. data @> '{"status":"active"}' is the canonical indexable JSONB filter.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: How do you index a JSONB column?
cards.a: A GIN index. The default operator class supports containment and key-existence; jsonb_path_ops builds a smaller, faster index supporting containment only.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: When is JSONB the right modelling choice?
cards.a: For genuinely schemaless data — a webhook payload stored verbatim, per-tenant custom fields, an LLM's raw response. It is wrong as a way to avoid designing a schema.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is the standard hybrid pattern?
cards.a: Real typed columns for everything the application filters, joins or constrains on, plus one jsonb column for the variable long tail.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is JSONPath in Postgres?
cards.a: A query language for navigating inside JSON documents, added in Postgres 12 — jsonb_path_query(data, '$.items[*].price ? (@ > 100)').

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: How do you turn a JSONB array into rows?
cards.a: jsonb_array_elements(data->'items') in a lateral join, which is how you aggregate or join against elements of a document.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What are Postgres arrays good for and where do they go wrong?
cards.a: Good for small, stable lists such as tags, queried with = ANY(...) and @> and indexed with GIN. Wrong when the "array" is really an entity with its own attributes, lifecycle or constraints — that is a table.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is an ENUM type, and what is the catch?
cards.a: A fixed set of allowed labels with compact storage. Adding a value is easy; removing one is genuinely painful, which is why many teams prefer a text column with a CHECK constraint or a lookup table.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: Why choose UUID over a bigint identity key?
cards.a: Clients can generate ids without a round trip, ids can be merged across systems, and they do not leak how many rows exist or let someone enumerate your data.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is the performance cost of random UUIDs as primary keys?
cards.a: They are random, so inserts scatter across the whole B-tree instead of appending at one end, causing page splits, poor cache locality and index bloat.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is UUIDv7 and why does it matter?
cards.a: A UUID with a timestamp in its high bits so values sort roughly by creation time, restoring append-like insert behaviour. Postgres 18 provides uuidv7() in core.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: Where does gen_random_uuid() come from?
cards.a: It was in the pgcrypto extension historically and moved into core in Postgres 13, so no extension is needed on modern versions.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What are range types?
cards.a: Types holding an interval as one value — tstzrange, daterange, int4range — with containment (@>) and overlap (&&) operators.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is an exclusion constraint and what can it guarantee?
cards.a: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&) guarantees no two rows for the same room have overlapping time ranges — an invariant that is genuinely hard to enforce in application code.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is a tsvector?
cards.a: The normalised, searchable form of a document: text broken into lexemes, stemmed ("running" to "run"), with stop words removed and positions recorded.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is a tsquery and which parser should you use for user input?
cards.a: The parsed search expression. Use websearch_to_tsquery for raw user input — it accepts quotes, or and - and never raises a syntax error, unlike to_tsquery.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: How do you match a document against a query?
cards.a: The @@ operator: WHERE search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1).

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: How do you make full-text search fast and self-maintaining?
cards.a: Store the tsvector in a generated column (Postgres 12+) so it updates itself, and put a GIN index on it.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What do ts_rank and ts_headline do?
cards.a: ts_rank scores how well a document matches, for ordering results; ts_headline returns a snippet with matched terms highlighted.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: Honestly, when is Postgres full-text search not enough?
cards.a: When you need sophisticated relevance tuning, fuzzy matching out of the box, faceting at scale, or search-specific scaling independent of the database. It is genuinely good enough to skip Elasticsearch for a large fraction of applications.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What does the pg_trgm extension add?
cards.a: Trigram similarity — a similarity() function and % operator for fuzzy matching and typo tolerance — and GIN/GiST support that makes LIKE '%foo%' and ILIKE indexable.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is a generated column?
cards.a: A column whose value is computed from other columns and maintained by the database — ideal for a search vector, a normalised email, or a computed total. Stored since Postgres 12; virtual (non-stored) added in 18.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What does date_trunc do and where is it used?
cards.a: Truncates a timestamp to a unit — date_trunc('day', created_at) — which is how you bucket time-series data for reports.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is generate_series useful for?
cards.a: Producing a table of values on demand — a row per day in a range, for example — which is the standard trick for filling gaps so a chart has zeroes rather than missing points.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is an interval?
cards.a: A duration type supporting arithmetic with timestamps — now() - interval '7 days'. Note that adding a month is calendar-aware, not a fixed number of seconds.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is the hstore type and why is it mostly historical?
cards.a: A flat string-to-string key-value type predating JSONB. JSONB supersedes it for essentially all new work.

cards.t: Node 14 · The types that make Postgres unusual
cards.q: What is a composite type?
cards.a: A named row type — CREATE TYPE address AS (street text, city text) — usable as a column type or as a function's return type. Powerful, but often better modelled as separate columns or a related table.

cards.q: What is a view, and what does it cost at runtime?
cards.a: A named query that behaves like a table. It stores nothing — selecting from it inlines its definition into your query — so it is an abstraction with no runtime cost and no caching.

cards.q: What are views genuinely good for?
cards.a: Hiding a complicated join behind a name, and exposing a restricted subset of a table to a role that has no permission on the underlying table.

cards.q: When is a view updatable?
cards.a: When it is simple enough for Postgres to map changes back unambiguously — a single table, no aggregates or DISTINCT. Otherwise you need an INSTEAD OF trigger.

cards.q: What is a materialized view?
cards.a: A view whose result is actually stored on disk and refreshed only when you run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. It makes an expensive aggregation instant to read at the price of being stale.

cards.q: What is the catch with refreshing a materialized view?
cards.a: Plain REFRESH takes an exclusive lock, blocking readers for the duration. REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY does not, but requires a unique index on the view and is slower.

cards.q: What is a CTE?
cards.a: A common table expression — WITH x AS (...) — that names a subquery, making long queries readable and letting a subquery be referenced more than once.

cards.q: How did CTE behaviour change in Postgres 12?
cards.a: Before 12, every CTE was an optimisation fence: always materialised, never inlined, and often exploited as a poor man's hint. From 12, a CTE referenced once and free of side effects is inlined by default; MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED force either behaviour.

cards.q: What is a recursive CTE for?
cards.a: Walking hierarchies and graphs in a single query — category trees, org charts, reachability — with WITH RECURSIVE: a base query UNIONed with a query that references the CTE itself.

cards.q: What is a window function?
cards.a: A function computing a value across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing the rows the way GROUP BY does.

cards.q: How do you get the most recent row per group with a window function?
cards.a: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) in a subquery, then filter to = 1 in the outer query.

cards.q: What is the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK?
cards.a: Both assign the same rank to ties; RANK then skips numbers (1,1,3) while DENSE_RANK does not (1,1,2).

cards.q: What do LAG and LEAD do?
cards.a: Return a value from the previous or next row in the window — the direct way to compute deltas, gaps between events, or "did this change from last time".

cards.q: How do you write a running total?
cards.a: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

cards.q: What is the difference between PARTITION BY and GROUP BY?
cards.a: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window computation while keeping every row in the output; GROUP BY collapses each group into one row.

cards.q: What is PL/pgSQL?
cards.a: Postgres's procedural language for functions — variables, conditionals, loops, exception handling — executed inside the server.

cards.q: What are the three volatility categories for a function and why do they matter?
cards.a: IMMUTABLE (same input always gives same output; required for expression indexes), STABLE (constant within one statement; can be used in index scans), and VOLATILE (the default; the planner can optimise nothing around it).

cards.q: What is the difference between a function and a procedure?
cards.a: Procedures, added in Postgres 11, can COMMIT and ROLLBACK internally, which functions cannot. That makes procedures the right tool for a batched backfill loop.

cards.q: What is a trigger?
cards.a: A function run automatically BEFORE or AFTER an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, either per row or per statement.

cards.q: What are triggers genuinely good for?
cards.a: Maintaining an updated_at timestamp, writing an audit log, and keeping a denormalised counter or search vector in step.

cards.q: Why are triggers a bad home for business logic?
cards.a: They are invisible at the call site. A developer reading the application code has no way to know that one insert also performed five other actions, and debugging becomes archaeology.

cards.q: What is the difference between a BEFORE and an AFTER trigger?
cards.a: A BEFORE trigger can modify the row about to be written (by returning a changed NEW) or cancel the operation by returning NULL. An AFTER trigger cannot change the row but sees the final state, which is what you want for auditing.

cards.q: What is LISTEN/NOTIFY?
cards.a: A lightweight pub/sub built into the server: one session runs LISTEN channel, another runs NOTIFY channel, 'payload', and the listener is woken.

cards.q: What makes NOTIFY transactionally correct?
cards.a: Notifications are delivered at commit, so a notification is never sent for a change that rolled back.

cards.q: What are the limits of LISTEN/NOTIFY?
cards.a: Payload capped at 8000 bytes, no persistence (a disconnected listener misses the message entirely), and it does not survive PgBouncer transaction pooling. Right for cache invalidation or nudging a worker; wrong when delivery must be guaranteed.

cards.q: What is row-level security?
cards.a: A policy attached to a table (Postgres 9.5+) that implicitly adds a WHERE clause to every query based on the current role or a session setting, making tenant isolation a property of the database rather than of every query.

cards.q: Sketch a row-level security policy for multi-tenancy.
cards.a: ALTER TABLE items ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; then CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON items USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid); with the application setting app.tenant_id per request.

cards.q: What is an extension?
cards.a: A packaged bundle of types, functions, operators, index operator classes and sometimes C code, installed into a database with CREATE EXTENSION name.

cards.q: Why can extensions add genuinely fast new capabilities rather than bolt-ons?
cards.a: Because Postgres's type, operator and index frameworks — particularly GiST and GIN — were designed from the Berkeley days to be extended, so an extension can add a new kind of data with a working index for it.

cards.q: Are extensions installed per server or per database?
cards.a: Per database. \dx lists what is installed in the database you are connected to.

cards.q: What is shared_preload_libraries and which extensions need it?
cards.a: A setting listing shared libraries loaded at server startup. Extensions that hook into the server itself — most importantly pg_stat_statements, and also auto_explain and pg_cron — require it, and therefore a restart.

cards.q: What does pg_stat_statements record?
cards.a: Every executed query, normalised so queries differing only in parameter values group together, with call count, total and mean time, rows returned, and buffer hit/read counts.

cards.q: Why is pg_stat_statements the single most valuable extension to install?
cards.a: Because ordering by total time answers the only question that matters when a database is slow — what is actually consuming this server — and the answer is very often a fast query run ten million times, not the slow one everyone is staring at.

cards.q: What is auto_explain?
cards.a: An extension that logs the execution plan of any query exceeding a duration threshold, so you get the plan of the slow production query rather than the plan of your reproduction attempt.

cards.q: What does pgvector add?
cards.a: A vector type, distance operators (<-> L2, <=> cosine, <#> inner product), and the IVFFlat and HNSW index types for approximate nearest-neighbour search.

cards.q: What does "approximate" mean for a vector index and what tunes it?
cards.a: The index may miss some true nearest neighbours in exchange for speed. IVFFlat is tuned by lists at build time and ivfflat.probes at query time; HNSW by m and ef_construction at build and hnsw.ef_search at query.

cards.q: Why keep embeddings in Postgres rather than a dedicated vector database?
cards.a: Because the embedding and the row it describes are written in the same transaction, removing an entire class of consistency problem, and because it is one system to back up, monitor and operate.

cards.q: What does pgcrypto provide?
cards.a: Hashing and symmetric/asymmetric encryption functions, and historically gen_random_uuid() before core absorbed it in Postgres 13.

cards.q: What is PostGIS?
cards.a: The geospatial extension — geometry and geography types, spatial indexing on GiST, and a very large function library. It is so complete that it is a major reason organisations choose Postgres at all.

cards.q: What is TimescaleDB for?
cards.a: Time-series workloads: automatic partitioning into "hypertables", columnar compression of older chunks, and continuous aggregates.

cards.q: What is Citus?
cards.a: An extension that distributes tables across multiple Postgres nodes — sharding, delivered as an extension rather than a fork.

cards.q: What is postgres_fdw?
cards.a: A foreign data wrapper making tables on another Postgres server queryable as if local, with a whole family of siblings for MySQL, files, S3 and REST APIs.

cards.q: What is pg_repack for?
cards.a: Removing table and index bloat online, without the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that makes VACUUM FULL an outage.

cards.q: What is pg_cron?
cards.a: An extension that runs scheduled SQL inside the database on a cron expression — useful for refreshing materialized views or pruning old rows without external infrastructure.

cards.q: What is the strategic argument for "just use Postgres"?
cards.a: Search, geospatial, vector similarity, time-series, job queues and pub/sub can all live in one system with one backup story, one transactional boundary and one operational burden — until scale genuinely forces specialisation.

cards.q: What limits extensions on managed Postgres?
cards.a: The provider allows only a fixed list, and anything requiring shared_preload_libraries or superuser cannot be added by you. Checking the supported-extensions list is part of choosing a provider.

cards.q: What is pg_stat_activity?
cards.a: One row per connection showing the current query, when it started, the connection state, and what it is waiting on. It is always the first place to look during an incident.

cards.q: What are the important values of state?
cards.a: active (running a query), idle (connected, doing nothing — fine), and idle in transaction (inside an open transaction doing nothing — the dangerous one).

cards.q: Write the query for "everything running longer than a minute".
cards.a: SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS dur, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '1 minute' ORDER BY dur DESC;

cards.q: What do wait_event_type and wait_event tell you?
cards.a: Why a backend is not running — Lock (waiting on another transaction), IO (reading from storage), LWLock (internal contention), Client (waiting on the application to send or receive).

cards.q: What does pg_stat_user_tables give you?
cards.a: Per table: sequential versus index scan counts, rows inserted/updated/deleted, live and dead tuple estimates, and last_autovacuum / last_autoanalyze.

cards.q: How do you spot a table that needs an index from pg_stat_user_tables?
cards.a: A high seq_scan count with a large seq_tup_read and a low idx_scan on a table that is not tiny.

cards.q: What does pg_stat_database give you?
cards.a: Per database: commits and rollbacks, blocks hit versus read (cache hit ratio), deadlock count, temp files written, and conflicts on standbys.

cards.q: How do you compute the cache hit ratio and what is a good value?
cards.a: blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read). Below roughly 99% on an OLTP workload suggests shared_buffers is too small for the working set — though the OS cache means the real picture is kinder than the number suggests.

cards.q: What is the highest-value logging setting?
cards.a: log_min_duration_statement — log every statement slower than, say, 500 ms. It turns "the site feels slow" into a list of specific queries.

cards.q: What do log_lock_waits, log_temp_files and log_checkpoints catch?
cards.a: Lock waits longer than deadlock_timeout, sorts and hashes spilling to disk (a work_mem signal), and checkpoint frequency and duration (a max_wal_size signal).

cards.q: What is shared_buffers conventionally set to?
cards.a: About 25% of system RAM. Much higher gives diminishing returns because the OS page cache is also caching the same files.

cards.q: What is effective_cache_size conventionally set to, and what does it allocate?
cards.a: 50–75% of RAM, and it allocates nothing. It only informs the planner how much caching to assume, which changes how attractive repeated index access looks.

cards.q: What is maintenance_work_mem for?
cards.a: VACUUM, index builds and ALTER TABLE. It can safely be far larger than work_mem — hundreds of megabytes to a gigabyte — because few maintenance operations run at once.

cards.q: How do you change a setting without editing a file?
cards.a: ALTER SYSTEM SET random_page_cost = 1.1; then SELECT pg_reload_conf(); — it writes postgresql.auto.conf. Some settings still require a restart.

cards.q: How do you tell whether a setting needs a restart?
cards.a: SELECT name, setting, context, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name = '...'. The context column says postmaster (restart), sighup (reload), or user (per-session).

cards.q: Why are Postgres's defaults so conservative?
cards.a: So it starts on any machine, including tiny ones. An untuned production server runs with 128 MB of buffers and 4 MB of work memory on a box with 64 GB of RAM — tuning is not exotic, it is the first hour of operating one.

cards.q: What is pg_stat_user_indexes used for?
cards.a: Finding indexes with idx_scan = 0 (unused, pure write cost) and comparing idx_scan against idx_tup_fetch to see how selective each index actually is in practice.

cards.q: How do you find the largest tables in a database?
cards.a: SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 20;

cards.q: What is the checklist when someone says "the database is slow"?
cards.a: Check pg_stat_activity for long-running and blocked queries; check pg_stat_statements ordered by total time; check connection count against max_connections; check n_dead_tup and last autovacuum; check disk and the logs for checkpoints and temp files.

cards.q: What is the difference between "the database is slow" and "the pool is exhausted"?
cards.a: They look identical from the application — requests hang. One is fixed in the database, the other in the application. This is why pool waiting-count belongs in your metrics.

cards.q: What should you monitor continuously on a production Postgres?
cards.a: Connection count, longest transaction age, replication lag, dead tuple counts and autovacuum recency, cache hit ratio, disk usage including pg_wal, deadlock rate, and the top queries by total time.

cards.q: What is track_io_timing?
cards.a: A setting that makes Postgres measure actual time spent in I/O, which is what fills in the timing numbers in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and pg_stat_statements. Worth enabling; the overhead is small on modern systems.

cards.q: Why does query timing in your application exceed the database's reported time?
cards.a: Network round trips, driver overhead, waiting for a connection from the pool, and result-set parsing. Postgres reports execution time, not end-to-end latency.

cards.q: What is the single best habit for keeping a database healthy?
cards.a: Look at pg_stat_statements ordered by total time once a week. Almost every emerging problem shows up there before it becomes an incident.

cards.q: What is a logical backup?
cards.a: pg_dump — a dump of SQL statements or a custom-format archive that recreates the data. Portable across versions and architectures, restorable table by table, and slow to restore at scale because everything is re-inserted and every index rebuilt.

cards.q: What is a physical backup?
cards.a: pg_basebackup (or pgBackRest, WAL-G) — a byte-level copy of the data directory. Restores fast, but only to a compatible major version and architecture.

cards.q: What is pg_dumpall for?
cards.a: Dumping cluster-wide objects that pg_dump does not include — roles, tablespaces, and global grants. A logical backup strategy needs both.

cards.q: What is point-in-time recovery?
cards.a: Restoring a physical base backup and then replaying archived WAL up to a chosen timestamp, giving you the database exactly as it was one second before a bad DELETE.

cards.q: What does PITR require to be set up in advance?
cards.a: Continuous WAL archiving — an archive_command (or an archive library) copying each completed WAL segment to durable storage — plus periodic base backups.

cards.q: What is the rule that outranks every backup strategy?
cards.a: A backup you have not restored is not a backup. Restore drills are the only evidence the process works.

cards.q: What are RPO and RTO?
cards.a: Recovery Point Objective — how much data you can afford to lose. Recovery Time Objective — how long you can afford to be down. They determine your backup frequency and your replication topology, and should be stated numbers.

cards.q: What is streaming replication?
cards.a: A primary streams its WAL to one or more standbys which continuously replay it, producing byte-identical copies. Introduced in Postgres 9.0.

cards.q: What is a hot standby?
cards.a: A standby that serves read-only queries while replaying, giving high availability and read scaling from the same mechanism.

cards.q: What is replication lag and why does it matter to application code?
cards.a: How far behind the standby is. Under default asynchronous replication it can be milliseconds or, under load, seconds — so an application that writes to the primary and immediately reads from a replica may not see its own write.

cards.q: What is the read-your-writes problem?
cards.a: A user saves something, is redirected, the read goes to a lagging replica, and their change appears not to have happened. It is why routing reads to replicas is an application-visible decision, not a transparent optimisation.

cards.q: What does synchronous replication change?
cards.a: With synchronous_commit = on plus synchronous_standby_names, the primary waits for a standby to acknowledge before returning COMMIT — eliminating the lag window and data loss on failover, at the cost of commit latency.

cards.q: What is the danger of synchronous replication with a single standby?
cards.a: If that standby dies, the primary has nobody to wait for and stops accepting writes. Production setups use quorum settings (ANY 1 (s1, s2)) rather than a single required standby.

cards.q: How do you measure replication lag?
cards.a: On the primary, pg_stat_replication shows write/flush/replay LSN positions per standby; on the standby, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() compared to now.

cards.q: What is a replication slot?
cards.a: A named marker on the primary recording how far a standby has consumed, so the primary retains the WAL that standby still needs. Powerful and dangerous: an abandoned slot retains WAL forever and fills the disk.

cards.q: What is the standby query conflict problem?
cards.a: A long query on a standby can need rows that WAL replay is about to remove. Postgres either cancels the query or delays replay. hot_standby_feedback = on tells the primary to hold vacuum back for the standby — fixing the queries and reintroducing bloat on the primary.

cards.q: What is failover, and does Postgres do it for you?
cards.a: Promoting a standby when the primary dies. Postgres does not do this itself; you need Patroni, repmgr, or a managed provider.

cards.q: What is split brain and why does failover need fencing?
cards.a: Two nodes both believing they are primary, accepting divergent writes. Avoiding it requires consensus and fencing the old primary — which is one honest reason to pay for managed Postgres.

cards.q: What is logical replication and how does it differ from streaming replication?
cards.a: It decodes the WAL into row-level changes and publishes them per table, via CREATE PUBLICATION and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION (Postgres 10+). Being logical rather than byte-level, it works across major versions and can replicate a subset of tables into a target with tables of its own.

cards.q: What is the standard use for logical replication?
cards.a: Near-zero-downtime major version upgrades, and change-data-capture feeds into analytics systems or Kafka.

cards.q: What is declarative partitioning?
cards.a: Splitting one logical table into many physical ones by range, list or hash (Postgres 10+). The parent holds no data; Postgres routes inserts and prunes partitions the query cannot need.

cards.q: What are the genuine wins of partitioning?
cards.a: Dropping old data becomes an instant DROP TABLE instead of a huge DELETE; vacuum, index builds and statistics operate on manageable pieces; and queries filtered on the partition key touch far less data.

cards.q: What does partitioning cost you?
cards.a: Every unique constraint must include the partition key, plans get larger with many partitions, and queries that do not filter on the partition key must touch all of them. It is not a general performance fix — for most tables a good index is better.

cards.q: What is sharding and when is it the right answer?
cards.a: Splitting data across separate servers, either with Citus or in the application. It is the right answer only after vertical scaling, read replicas, partitioning and query fixes are genuinely exhausted — which is much later than most people assume.

cards.q: What do you give up with managed Postgres?
cards.a: Superuser, arbitrary shared_preload_libraries, and extensions outside the provider's list. You gain backups, failover, patching and monitoring.

cards.q: What does "RDS Multi-AZ" actually mean?
cards.a: Synchronous physical replication to a standby in another availability zone, with automatic failover. The standby is not readable in the classic Multi-AZ configuration.

cards.q: What is different about Neon and Aurora architecturally?
cards.a: They separate storage from compute, so compute can scale to zero or scale out independently, and features like instant database branching become possible.

cards.q: What is the difference between vertical scaling and read replicas as a first response to load?
cards.a: Vertical scaling helps every workload and requires no application change; read replicas help only read-heavy workloads and force you to reason about staleness. Vertical first is usually correct.

cards.q: What is a driver?
cards.a: The library that speaks Postgres's wire protocol from your language. In Node the two real choices are pg (the long-standing standard, with pg.Pool) and postgres.js (newer, faster, tagged-template API).

cards.q: Why does the pg driver return bigint and numeric as strings?
cards.a: Because they do not fit safely in a JavaScript number — precision would be silently lost. You must convert deliberately, which is the correct default.

cards.q: What does the driver do with a Postgres date or timestamp?
cards.a: Converts it to a JavaScript Date, interpreted in the server or client timezone depending on the type, which is a common source of off-by-one-day bugs. Many teams configure the driver to return dates as strings.

cards.q: How do you write a parameterised query in node-postgres?
cards.a: client.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]). Postgres numbers parameters $1, $2 rather than using ?.

cards.q: Why is string concatenation into SQL the vulnerability?
cards.a: Because user input becomes part of the parsed query text, so a value can become syntax — closing a quote and appending OR 1=1 or a second statement. Parameters are transmitted separately and never parsed as SQL.

cards.q: How do you safely handle a dynamic ORDER BY column from a user?
cards.a: Validate it against an allow-list of permitted column names and map to a literal in your code. Identifiers cannot be parameterised.

cards.q: Write the correct shape of a transaction in application code.
cards.a: Acquire a client from the pool, BEGIN, do the work, COMMIT; in catch, ROLLBACK; in finally, release the client.

cards.q: What happens if you forget to release a pooled client?
cards.a: You leak a connection. Leak enough and the pool is exhausted, requests queue forever, and the application deadlocks against itself with no error visible on the database side.

cards.q: Why must you never await a slow external call inside a transaction?
cards.a: It pins a connection, holds every lock the transaction has taken, and blocks the vacuum horizon for the whole duration. Do the HTTP call or the LLM completion outside the transaction.

cards.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
cards.a: Fetching a list of N rows and then issuing one query per row for a related record — 101 round trips where one join or one WHERE id = ANY($1) would do.

cards.q: How does each ORM let you avoid N+1?
cards.a: Prisma's include/select for eager loading; Drizzle's relational query API or an explicit join. The skill is knowing to look for it, which means seeing the generated SQL.

cards.q: What is the single fastest way to learn what your ORM is doing?
cards.a: Turn on query logging for a day and read the SQL it generates for your real endpoints. Every ORM has the switch.

cards.q: What is the professional stance on ORMs?
cards.a: Use the ORM for the large majority of queries that are trivial, drop to raw parameterised SQL for the ones that matter, and always be able to see the generated SQL.

cards.q: Why can an ORM produce a much slower query than the obvious hand-written one?
cards.a: It may select every column (including TOASTed ones), add unnecessary joins or subqueries to satisfy its object model, or generate a shape the planner handles worse than the direct equivalent.

cards.q: Which errors must an application retry, and how?
cards.a: SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure) and 40P01 (deadlock detected) — retry the whole transaction with exponential backoff and a bounded attempt count.

cards.q: What makes a retry unsafe?
cards.a: Side effects outside the database. If the transaction sent an email or charged a card, replaying it repeats that. Retries require the work to be idempotent or the external effect to be moved outside.

cards.q: What is an idempotency key and where does it live?
cards.a: A client-supplied unique token stored in a table with a unique constraint, so a repeated request finds the existing row instead of doing the work twice. It is how you make an API endpoint safely retryable.

cards.q: Why should statement_timeout be set at the application role level?
cards.a: So no query from the application can run forever regardless of what any individual developer remembered, while admin sessions retain the ability to run long maintenance.

cards.q: What should you expose in metrics to distinguish database problems from pool problems?
cards.a: The pool's in-use and waiting counts, plus the database's connection count and longest transaction age. Without them, "slow" is indistinguishable from "starved".

cards.q: What is connection churn and why does it matter?
cards.a: Opening and closing connections repeatedly rather than reusing pooled ones. Each cycle costs a fork and authentication, and it shows up as high CPU on the database with no expensive queries.

cards.q: What is the right way to run a large read that would exhaust memory in Node?
cards.a: A cursor or streaming query (pg-cursor, or postgres.js's streaming API), fetching in batches — never SELECT of ten million rows into an array.

cards.q: Why do prepared statements sometimes break behind a pooler and what is the fix?
cards.a: In transaction pooling mode the next statement may land on a different backend that has never seen the prepared statement. The fix is disabling server-side prepares in the driver.

cards.q: What does a healthy database access layer look like in one sentence?
cards.a: One pool created at startup with a small max, every query parameterised, transactions short and free of external calls, timeouts set, serialization and deadlock errors retried, and the generated SQL visible.

cards.q: Which Postgres problems will you personally cause most often?
cards.a: Not planner problems — N+1 queries, leaked connections, transactions held open across network calls, and missing indexes on foreign keys. Almost all of them live in application code, not in the database.
